Hacknet is, as the title implies, a hacking video game developed by Matt Trobbiani, stemming from a 48-hour game jam idea built into a full game throughout two and a half years. Playing as an unnamed hacker, you are called into the fray to investigate the death of a prominent hacker after downloading Hacknet, a new operating system designed specifically to exploit security issues in consumer servers.

Hacknet's story exists solely to give the player something to do other than poke around. It doesn't get going until halfway through the game, and by then you'd probably have forgotten the initial premise like me. Nevertheless, it's not bad at all, and there is a mildly interesting mystery for the player to solve. What's more interesting are the little side stories you can find just by poking around in the game. A screenwriter who wants to sell his terrible script to a movie exec, a man who is so addicted to an online idle game that he wants you to reset his score, and even a family begging to have their patriarch's heart monitor shut off. There are also small little IRC chat archives you can find, and they tend to be pretty funny too. The problem is that they tend to be repeated numerous times and after a while can lose a bit of their luster. Being a voyeur is a concept I have always found very interesting in gaming and Hacknet lets you excel at that.

The actual gameplay consists of, well, hacking. I have no idea how realistic the actual hacking mechanics are, but Trobbiani did a very good job of making them feel immersive. Everything is designed exactly like a real OS (highly simplified, of course) with command prompt and all. It's essentially a puzzle game, with the player using their newly acquired programs to approach increasingly difficult puzzles. Using a command prompt as your main weapon is a lovely idea and it plays out very well, adding to the immersion much more than Windows-style icons could have. The number of things you have to discover and the different ways you can discover them is insanely impressive and it feels as if an immersive sim and a text adventure game had a baby. My only complaint is that the side missions can become very repetitive, and they don't have a consistently increasing scale of challenge, making some of them feel like busywork instead of your next big heist. Trobbiani does try to add variety, such as having another hacker try to hack you for a change, but this variation does not occur as frequently as I'd like.

It's hard to say anything about the presentation considering the game consists primarily of text, but I'll say Trobbiani achieves the look of a fictionalized OS pretty well. You can activate certain visual effects like bloom and scanlines to make it resemble an old monitor, and these are nice small touches. The soundtrack is often praised but I'm afraid it didn't resonate with me. It's mostly fine but it's a pretty generic electronic score and after a while, I just muted it because I found it actively took away from the immersion for me. I understand why people love it but it just wasn't for me.

Hacknet is a very innovative title and one of the most creative indie games I've played as of late. Sure, it suffers from occasionally repetitive gameplay and storytelling, as well as a mediocre soundtrack, but the puzzle design, immersion, and raw sandbox-esque use of your abilities pull it forward. Not for everyone, but if it sounds remotely interesting to you, I'd recommend it.

[b] Amazing, clever indie game that succeeds in conveying that cool hacker power fantasy [b]

I got this game in a Humble Charity Bundle and the good reviews made me curious. I had it installed for years now and finally started it when in quarantine. And I am more than glad that I did! After a few moments of uncertainty due to the terminal-based gameplay, the game quickly won me over with its almost perfect difficulty balance, developping story, attention to detail and many, many fun secrets to find!
I would never have thought that this would be the kind of game for me but I ended loving every minute of playing through it over the period of 2-3 days, 100%ing it. I even played the equally magnificent DLC for some additional challenges and took some extra turns trying to find everything. It is one of those games where I wish I could experience it for the first time again!
The core gameplay loop is that the player receives various nodes (PCs, servers, etc.) which he then has to hack but certainly presented much more sophisticated than that! Hacks require different approaches and an ever-increasing array of increasingly powerful tools. They start very simple and become more and more complex. Over time they also require somewhat of detective work, if you will. I am more of a simpleton in regards to computer engineering but Hacknet made me feel super smart frequently when I found another piece of information or secret tool or when I finally understood a new instrument and figured out how to proceed. I would even go so far as to say that I actually learned a bit how to navigate in Linux; but I am probably wrong. However, 10/10 for conveying that power fantasy so good that I even overestimate my non-existent Linux experience in real life! :D The game keeps expanding - both in gameplay and story - without dragging and finds an appropriate and satisfying ending, I found.
The writing is much better than I expected and more than above average. It ended up becoming one of my favourite elements of the game and really motivated me to explore and find all the additional secrets! The attention to detail the dev put into this projects oozes out of every node, file, conversation piece and secret the player finds, rewarding curiosity and initiative.
I could praise the game on and on but I will come to an end now. I just want to thank the dev for creating this gem and showing me once again why I love the indie game scene so much! Buy the game and make sure to add the DLC, too. Seriously, the DLC is adding to the cleverness and challenge of the main game and I am more than glad I included it in my playthrough from the start.
Thank you and have fun!

Hacknet is fun and has a nice soundtrack. The story is OK and the puzzles aren't very challenging except for that one... but maybe I'm just not very smart. The game is also quite short, I was done with it in like 6 or so hours.

Hacking works like so: you have a set of "keys" - programs you run to break the "locks" on a system before you can PortHack into it to get control over that node. You start without any "key" and get them as you progress through the story.
The story is given to you through emails you receive in-game, and you advance it by doing tasks from specific people or special quest boards.
The difficulty is... You always have all the info and tools you need to deal with your current puzzles. Remember this. Sometimes people even remind you how some (easier) things are done. Then there's that one (avoidable, you may not trigger it) thing where you have to do something completely new which you got no instructions for. Or maybe I'm just dumb.
The game also quotes bash.org a lot.

Overall a very good introduction to usage of a basic terminal. All the commands that are not fictional are obviously derived from Linux/Unix. While this game obviously makes hacking a trivial ordeal, it's still mostly realistic in the sense of only being able to use a certain amount of programs at once due to limited memory, correct SSH, HTTP, FTP, and so on port numbers, and the use of NMap. I highly recommend this game if you enjoy playing around with networking, ethical(or maybe even unethical) hacking, the use of terminals, and retro-style computer games.

I have played a fair amount of various "hacking games" on steam, and this is honestly one of the best of those that I have played.

  With an actually intriguing and lore filled story, hidden (and not) gimmicks, and unique twists, the game keeps you wanting more.
  Hacknet takes a more realistic, but not too realistic approach, that manages to make it reflect computer systems and networks more accurately, while still feeling like a game.
  While not at all required, background knowledge on some things, especially terminals, network layouts, ipv4 formatting, linux/unix based system filesystems did come in handy for me.

I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a game of this genre, as it keeps a good balance of difficulty in different aspects.
While still obviously a game, this simulation is about as real as it could be without turning off people who don't want to have to study too much, and more realistic than most movie hacking scenes.

[h1]A well written tale, an unexpected turn of events[/h1]
Just finished the game. Will go through the DLC later while finishing the couple achievements I have left.

Really a great experience. Cleverly written, puts you in the mind of a hacker who has to go through minor routine tasks which rapidly evolve into the morally questionable territory.

As a Linux enthusiast and daily user, I must say I appreciated the many references the game holds to these communities. Although, when I first played it back in 2017, I had a rough time handling the terminal and that really made the core gameplay quite difficult to handle.

Otherwise, the storytelling is great, the visuals are well-made, the game itself is immersive and plays well with the imminent danger factor. Plus, the soundtrack is pure gold, and contributes a lot to the atmosphere.

Finally, and despite the "C00L H@CKERZ" appearance it might have, its minimalism proves to be effective when you are dealt with difficult moral decisions, unlike many other games which feature a hacking theme.

Will update this review when I play through the DLC.
